cards.title: Competitive equilibrium for almost all budgets with two additive agents
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: For every m≥1 and every pair of positive additive valuations on m indivisible goods, is the set of positive budget pairs (b₁,b₂) for which no competitive equilibrium exists a set of two-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero?
cards.why: Tests whether a small asymmetry in purchasing power is enough to recover equilibrium with indivisible goods.

cards.definitions: The goods are M=[m]. For i∈{1,2}, finite real numbers v_i,g>0 define v_i(S)=∑_{g∈S}v_i,g for every S⊆M. Different bundles may have equal value. Budgets b₁,b₂ are arbitrary positive real numbers. A price vector assigns each good a real price p_g≥0, with p(S)=∑_{g∈S}p_g. A competitive equilibrium consists of p and a partition (A₁,A₂) of M, allowing an empty bundle, such that p(A_i)≤b_i and v_i(A_i)≥v_i(S) for every S⊆M with p(S)≤b_i, for both agents simultaneously. All goods must be allocated once. Agents value only their goods: unspent budget has no utility and need not be exhausted. Ties among best affordable bundles are permitted. For each fixed valuation pair, its exceptional set lies in (0,∞)² and must have Lebesgue measure zero, meaning it can be covered by countably many rectangles whose total area is smaller than any prescribed ε>0. The exceptional set may depend on the valuations. The allocation and prices may depend on the valuations and budgets. This is an exact existence statement with no running-time or finite-encoding requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the exceptional budget set has measure zero for every finite positive additive two-agent instance, or give one such instance and prove that its nonexistence set has positive two-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Failure at a single budget pair, including equal budgets, is insufficient for a negative answer; approximate clearing or a result confined to near-equal budgets is insufficient for a positive answer.

context_blocks.title: Why equal budgets can fail
context_blocks.text: Suppose both agents value one good positively and each has budget 1. At any price at most 1 both can afford and prefer the good, but only one can receive it; at a price above 1 neither can buy it. If the budgets become 1 and 1.01, a price of 1.005 gives a competitive equilibrium: only the richer agent can afford the good. This simple example explains why an exceptional line of budget pairs may be allowed.

context_blocks.title: What almost all means
context_blocks.text: The question covers budgets with arbitrarily unequal purchasing power as well as nearly equal ones. It permits a set of failures with zero area, rather than requiring existence at every pair or merely at many sampled pairs. A positive answer would mean that a budget pair drawn from any continuous density avoids the exceptional set with probability one.

context_blocks.title: The gap beyond known cases
context_blocks.text: Babaioff, Nisan and Talgam-Cohen establish existence for two additive agents with sufficiently close unequal budgets, and generic existence for identical preferences under their stated preference conventions. Segal-Halevi’s account gives almost-all existence with at most four goods and leaves the arbitrary additive case with five or more goods open. Failure examples for more general monotone preferences do not automatically give additive counterexamples.

context_blocks.title: Prices as allocation rules
context_blocks.text: Budgets represent purchasing entitlements and prices coordinate which bundles are simultaneously affordable. The target retains exact allocation of every good and exact optimality for each agent. Adding utility for cash, allowing unsold goods or replacing each whole good by fractions produces a different market.

sentences: Two agents use positive budgets to buy indivisible goods at common item prices.
Each must receive a most valuable affordable bundle, and every good must be allocated.
The question asks whether every positive additive valuation pair has an equilibrium outside a zero-area set of budget pairs.
Equal budgets can fail even for one good, while nearby unequal budgets and several other restricted cases are understood.
The unresolved target covers arbitrary numbers of goods and budgets that may be far from equal.

cards.context:
Suppose both agents value one good positively and each has budget 1. At any price at most 1 both can afford and prefer the good, but only one can receive it; at a price above 1 neither can buy it. If the budgets become 1 and 1.01, a price of 1.005 gives a competitive equilibrium: only the richer agent can afford the good. This simple example explains why an exceptional line of budget pairs may be allowed.

The question covers budgets with arbitrarily unequal purchasing power as well as nearly equal ones. It permits a set of failures with zero area, rather than requiring existence at every pair or merely at many sampled pairs. A positive answer would mean that a budget pair drawn from any continuous density avoids the exceptional set with probability one.

Babaioff, Nisan and Talgam-Cohen establish existence for two additive agents with sufficiently close unequal budgets, and generic existence for identical preferences under their stated preference conventions. Segal-Halevi’s account gives almost-all existence with at most four goods and leaves the arbitrary additive case with five or more goods open. Failure examples for more general monotone preferences do not automatically give additive counterexamples.

Budgets represent purchasing entitlements and prices coordinate which bundles are simultaneously affordable. The target retains exact allocation of every good and exact optimality for each agent. Adding utility for cash, allowing unsold goods or replacing each whole good by fractions produces a different market.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.

benchmark_selection.basis: Individual editorial review of saved titles, importance rationales, problem statements, source notes and working summaries.
